P34m: If these communities are supposed to spread, somebody eventually has to solve the boring problem of how they stay connected without turning into a super-commune (that's essentially just another state, with a nicer logo). I'd like them to connect, help each other and move people and knowledge around, but also to stay distinct enough that they can learn from one another. At the federation level, that outward purpose gets concrete: spreading healing practices, training people, seeding new projects, and keeping any one comfortable enclave from thinking it's the whole movement.
P4e: Once there's a federation, that outward purpose stops being abstract. You spread healing practices, you train people, you seed new projects. And you keep any one comfortable enclave from thinking it's the whole movement.
P6e2: On a related point, cooperation also shouldn't quietly turn into merging. The FEC has full members and communities working towards becoming full members, and it also has Friends who may simply stay friends. People need the same practical freedom of movement between communities. If somebody can move in theory, but nobody's sorted out where they'll live or what their status is, or their health coverage and records, how their labor gets counted, who pays for the travel, the taxes, and what happens if the move turns into a dispute, then that freedom is decorative. Often a thin interface does it, one that says who's responsible for what while somebody crosses between them, without every community's internal systems having to match.
P8e: And when two principles collide, don't just keep the final rule. Keep the hard case too. Write down what happened and which principles actually conflicted. Keep the first judgments, and the reasoning behind the final one, and any dissent. Note what the consequences were and exactly which version of the rule it was. When the rule changes, rerun the case. Otherwise each generation gets to rediscover the same constitutional fight from scratch.
P8f: When two principles collide, it's not enough to save the final rule. You need the hard case too, with what happened, which principles were really in conflict, what people first judged, why they finally decided the way they did, who dissented, what happened as a result, and which version of the rule it was. When the rule changes, you run the case again, or every generation ends up rediscovering the same constitutional fight from scratch.
P4f: At the level of federation, that outward purpose gets concrete: we want to be spreading our healing practices, training people, seeding new projects, and making sure the people settling into nice enclaves don't think their enclave is the whole movement.
P6g: One thing to notice about cooperating is that it shouldn't quietly turn into merging. The FEC has full members and communities working towards becoming full members, plus "Friends" who may never do more than be friends. Related to this, we need to let people move from one community to another, and not just in theory. In practice that means housing, status, health coverage, records, labor accounting, travel costs, taxes, and dealing with disputes that come up at transition time, or the freedom is only decorative. Often a thin interface can do this, one that says who's responsible for what while somebody crosses between them, and the different systems the communities have internally don't all have to be the same.
P8g: When you create a rule to deal with a collision of two principles, don't only store the rule. Store the hard case too: what happened, the principles involved, your first judgments, your final decision and rationale, any dissenting opinions, the consequences, and which version of the rule it was decided under. When the rule changes, run the case through again. That saves each generation from having to rediscover the same constitutional fight from scratch.
P8h: When a conflict between two principles leads to a rule, don't only keep the rule. Keep the original case on file too: what happened, what principles were involved, what judgments were made first, what was finally decided and the rationale, what the dissenting opinions were, what the consequences were, and under what version of the rule it was decided. When the rule changes, re-run the case. Otherwise every generation gets to rediscover the same constitutional fight from scratch.
